title: How Election Workers Test Voting Machines Before Ballots Are Counted
summary:
The midterm elections end on Election Day in November, but in many states people are already voting. For the local officials who run elections, the work started even earlier. A PBS NewsHour report visited election offices to show how they get ready.

In Davis County, Utah, workers run stacks of practice ballots through the counting machines before a single real ballot is counted. Some of the test ballots are filled out wrong on purpose. This is called logic and accuracy testing. It checks that the machines count votes correctly and catch mistakes, such as a voter choosing too many candidates.

Utah is one of a few states where most people vote by mail. County clerk Brian McKenzie explained the path a mail ballot takes. Every envelope has its own bar code. If a voter needs a new ballot, the old code is canceled, so no one can get more than one. At least two workers pick up returned ballots, and the ballots are kept under video cameras around the clock.

Each envelope is scanned, stamped with the date and photographed. Workers compare the voter's signature with up to five signatures on file. Ballots move in batches of 200 and are counted at every step. McKenzie said nothing in the system is wireless or connected to the internet.

This year there was a fight in Washington over voting by mail. New Postal Service rules for mail ballots were announced at President Trump's direction, but the Supreme Court blocked them last month. McKenzie said voters can adjust to changes when they have enough time, but sudden changes close to an election can cause confusion and doubt.
why_it_matters: Trust in elections depends on people understanding how votes are checked and counted, and these steps show the safeguards officials use before results are announced.

background_read: In the United States, elections are run by local officials in counties and towns, not by one national office.
Before ballots are counted, election offices test their machines to make sure each vote is read correctly.
Some states let most voters mail in their ballots, so officials use bar codes and signature checks to make sure each voter sends only one ballot.
Midterm elections choose members of Congress and many state and local leaders halfway through a president's term.
